query: For high-entropy-alloy bond coats used in thermal barrier coating systems for high-temperature applications, what single intervention could improve coating durability and reliability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the aluminum content in a high-entropy alloy bond coat will improve the durability and reliability of thermal barrier coating systems by promoting the in‐flight formation of a dense, adherent Al2O3 scale that limits deleterious Mn depletion during high-temperature oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional CrMnFeCoNi HEA bond coat with a lower Al content that, under high-temperature oxidizing conditions, tends to form nonuniform oxide layers with significant Mn depletion.
generation.intervention: Increase the Al content in the bond coat composition prior to HVOF deposition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation conditions typical of thermal barrier coating operations (e.g., air atmosphere at temperatures up to 1100 °C) using HVOF processing parameters where in-flight oxidation can take place.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, dense, and well-adherent Al2O3 scale that forms in-flight during deposition.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced Al content drives controlled Al diffusion to the particle surface during HVOF, resulting in the preferential formation of a protective alumina scale that acts as a barrier against further oxidation, thereby reducing the accelerated oxidation of Mn and stabilizing the alloy’s microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified bond coat will exhibit slower oxidation kinetics, reduced Mn depletion at the scale–substrate interface, and overall improved adhesion and durability compared to the untreated HEA bond coat.
generation.baseline: Performance of the standard, lower-Al-content HEA bond coat under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions, which typically forms nonuniform oxide scales and suffers from Mn depletion.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected under high oxygen partial pressures and rapid thermal cycles characteristic of HVOF deposition and service in thermal barrier coating systems; deviations in oxygen availability or deposition parameters may alter the formation and stability of the Al2O3 scale.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of durability improvement and optimal Al content increase remain uncertain and may depend on specific HVOF processing conditions and service environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA bond coats via HVOF deposition: one using the conventional CrMnFeCoNi composition and the other with an increased Al content in the feedstock. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation cycles (e.g., thermal cycling up to 1100 °C in air) and perform in situ and ex situ analyses.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional SEM/EDS)
Degree of Mn depletion near the scale–substrate interface (via EDS elemental mapping)
Coating adhesion and spallation resistance (via standardized adhesion and durability tests)
Oxidation kinetics (mass gain measurements over time)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the increased Al content coatings do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxide uniformity, reduced Mn depletion, and enhanced adhesion/durability over the untreated baseline under controlled high-temperature conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 7c shows the cross-section topography after high-temperature XRD oxidation in air. An irregular oxide scale formed and remained adherent to the substrate. The oxide scale thickness is about 1.58, 2.53, and 3.45 μm at different locations, which indicates that oxidation does not occur uniformly on the surface. Furthermore, no evidence of internal oxidation attack along the grain boundaries within the substrate was observed. In addition, no internal oxidation attack in the substrate is seen as having been executed along the grain boundaries. Figure 8 presents a cross-sectional EDS map of the specimen oxidized when heated during in situ XRD. For the specimen oxidized, it was observed that a mixed oxide layer consisting of Mn, Cr, and Fe oxides on the substrate and the oxides were confirmed to be Mn2O3, Mn3O4, Fe3Mn3O8, and MnCr2O4 when combined with XRD data shown in Figure 6. Mn- and Cr-depleted areas formed in the scale–substrate interface area, which are now filled with a high concentration of Ni, Co, and Fe. Kim et al. One of the most promising applications of AlCoCrFeNi HEA is the fabrication of protective coatings [,]. HEA-based coatings, deposited on medium-carbon steel substrates, can considerably enhance the material performances, extend service life, and reduce product costs [,,]. Thick coatings with low porosity and a high level of adhesion can be produced via the high velocity fuel spraying (HVOF) technique [,]. HVOF is a combustion spray process in which a hydrocarbon fuel (kerosene, methane, propane, etc.) is ignited, mixing with oxygen to accelerate feedstock powder towards the substrate [,]. Depending on the particle’s size and location in the high-temperature flow, the particles undergo various transformations, such as melting, softening, spheroidization, precipitation, and surface or total oxidation, similar to those observed with the atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) method []. Lower particle temperatures than those achieved in plasma spraying and higher particle speeds result in lower in-flight particle oxidation and better coating densities.

Oxidation and phase transformations of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 high-entropy alloy powder produced via gas atomization were studied under HVOF deposition, during continuous heating, and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. The following was found:Under HVOF spraying, the processes of oxidation and phase transformations occur in the following sequence: (i) pronounced Al diffusion from subsurface BCC supersaturated solid solution to the particle surface; (ii) particle’s surface Al2O3 formation; and (iii) FCC formation in the Al-depleted subsurface layer.During continuous heating in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) Al diffusion to the surface; and (iii) simultaneous formation of Al2O3 and FCC due to Al outflow from BCC/B2.During prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C in an air atmosphere, processes occur in the following sequence: (i) decomposition of the BCC supersaturated solid solution with sigma formation; (ii) diffusion of Al, Cr, Fe, and Mo to the surface; and (iii) formation of surface Al2O3 and undersurface sigma due to enrichment of the undersurface zone with Cr

reading.lever: Increase Al content in the HEA bond coat to induce controlled in-flight formation of a dense, adherent Al2O3 scale.
reading.why: Al addition, as evidenced in HVOF coatings of related HEAs, yields a stable protective oxide that mitigates Mn depletion and enhances durability under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
